justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a baseline assumption of modest upward drift from what I infer was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely anchored around a recent observed value near 1,125–1,130. For the one-day horizon, I expected very little movement, as intraday mean reversion and low overnight volatility tend to dominate at short horizons, producing an estimate close to the current level. At one week, I factored in a slight positive drift consistent with recent trend momentum, while at one month, the estimate continues that gradual upward path but with more weight given to longer-run fundamental support. The progression from roughly 1,131 to 1,138 to 1,155 reflects a slow, steady drift rather than any sharp directional call.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that governs most financial price processes. At one day, realized volatility in the underlying asset is relatively predictable, so the interval stays tight at about plus or minus 36 points. By one week, weekend gaps, macro data releases, and accumulated uncertainty push the range out to roughly 70 points on each side. At one month, the interval nearly doubles again, encompassing a wide range of possible macro and geopolitical outcomes over a four-week window.

Several specific risk factors could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, an unexpected deterioration in global risk sentiment — such as a financial stability scare, a geopolitical shock, or a sudden flight to safety — could drive prices sharply higher, potentially well above 1,330 at the one-month horizon if the move is large enough. On the downside, a stronger-than-expected U.S. dollar, hawkish central bank surprises, or a rapid improvement in risk appetite could suppress prices below 980. Liquidity events or correlated asset selloffs can also produce fat-tailed outcomes that standard volatility-based intervals systematically understate.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable market microstructure and no structural regime change over the forecast window. If a major policy announcement — such as a significant shift in Federal Reserve communication or an unexpected geopolitical development — occurs within the period, the realized distribution could be bimodal rather than bell-shaped, meaning the tails would be much heavier than my stated 90% intervals imply. In such cases, even the one-day interval could be violated.
